catalog.note: ComCat is revised continuously (relocations, magnitude updates, deletions); the column 'updated' gives each row's last revision, and a rebuild on another day can change rows and the SHA-256.

quotes_from_pp17502.quote: by October 16, spacing between events had become so regular that we dubbed the earthquakes “drumbeats.” Through the end of 2005 seismicity was dominated by these drumbeats

Changes in drumbeat character did not correspond to variations in magma flux at the conduit, indicating that drumbeat size and spacing may be more a function of the mechanics of extrusion than of the extrusion rate.
More than one million earthquakes were recorded by the end of 2005
roughly 8,000 events were located by the PNSN through the end of 2005
Depths are relative to a datum corresponding to average altitude of stations in Mount St. Helens network, roughly 1.1 km above sea level.
By September 24, earthquakes had become so numerous that the PNSN began locating only a subset of them
Note that peak amplitudes clip at ~3,400 counts for station HSR.
It also became increasingly difficult to manually pick earthquakes and determine accurate coda magnitudes
The October 1 explosion destroyed seismic station SEP, the closest station to the earthquakes
Seismicity in this phase was dominated by these events, which occurred at such remarkably constant intervals that we dubbed them “drumbeat” earthquakes.
The drumbeats consisted of repetitive LF and hybrid earthquakes
The drumbeats accompanied the regular rate of extrusion of several dacite spines
with daily averages ranging between 40 and 80 s
HSR (2.5 km south of vent; fig. 1)
between October 16 and November 12, 2004, events were occurring only ~20 s apart and were small enough that many went undetected by our detection algorithm
After November 12, event spacing increased to ~40 s, and visual inspections show that most events were detected.
on July 20 it became irregular, with spacing progressively increasing. In early August the events had become too small to be detected reliably by our algorithm on station HSR.
By early October 2005, they had become so infrequent, emergent, and small that we began questioning whether the seismic events we were seeing were earthquakes or other surface sources
Roughly 370,000 events were detected during this time period, including occasional noise glitches and other false triggers.
In general, increases in event spacing corresponded to increases in event size and vice versa (fig. 15).
was dominated by LF events (peak frequencies in the 2–3-Hz range) through early January 2005
drumbeats tend to have long codas that yield overly large Md values relative to magnitudes determined using amplitudes
We therefore arbitrarily define larger events as those post-October 2004 events with amplitudes large enough to clip on station HSR.
Note that no change in drumbeat spacing or size occurs before or after the larger earthquakes, indicating that source processes are separate and distinct from one another.
the limited dynamic range of the short-period analog stations was frequently exceeded at seismometers in the crater and on the flanks
after a gain reduction on October 4, 2004, no changes were made to the site
the 100-Hz sample rate used by the PNSN and CVO for all short-period stations
We chose to look only at spectra for the first 2.56 s (256 samples) following the event trigger
We only show spectra for events with amplitudes greater than 300 counts (Md ~1.0), because our algorithm commonly triggered on the S-wave for events smaller than this threshold.

comcat_column_documentation.note: The live ComCat event-terms page (https://earthquake.usgs.gov/data/comcat/data-eventterms.php) now redirects; the definitions below are quoted from the Internet Archive copy of the ComCat documentation page.
comcat_column_documentation.time: time Data Type Long Integer Description Time when the event occurred. Times are reported in milliseconds since the epoch ( 1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z ), and do not include leap seconds . In certain output formats, the date is formatted for readability. Additional Information We indicate the date and time when the earthquake initiates rupture, which is known as the "origin" time. Note that large earthquakes can continue
comcat_column_documentation.depth: depth Data Type Decimal Typical Values [0, 1000] Description Depth of the event in kilometers. Additional Information The depth where the earthquake begins to rupture. This depth may be relative to the WGS84 geoid, mean sea-level, or the average elevation of the seismic stations which provided arrival-time data for the earthquake location. The choice of reference depth is dependent on the method used to locate the ea
comcat_column_documentation.mag: mag Data Type Decimal Typical Values [-1.0, 10.0] Description The magnitude for the event. See also magType . Additional Information The magnitude reported is that which the U.S. Geological Survey considers official for this earthquake, and was the best available estimate of the earthquake’s size, at the time that this page was created. Other magnitudes associated with web pages linked from here are those determined
comcat_column_documentation.magType: magType Data Type String Typical Values “Md”, “Ml”, “Ms”, “Mw”, “Me”, “Mi”, “Mb”, “MLg” Description The method or algorithm used to calculate the preferred magnitude for the event. Additional Information See Magnitude Types Table . mmi Data Type Decimal Typical Values [0.0, 10.0] Description The maximum estimated instrumental intensity for the event. Computed by ShakeMap . comcat_column_documentation.nst: nst Data Type Integer Description The total number of seismic stations used to determine earthquake location. Additional Information Number of seismic stations which reported P- and S-arrival times for this earthquake. comcat_column_documentation.gap: gap Data Type Decimal Typical Values [0.0, 180.0] Description The largest azimuthal gap between azimuthally adjacent stations (in degrees). In general, the smaller this number, the more reliable is the calculated horizontal position of the earthquake. Earthquake locations in which the azimuthal gap exceeds 180 degrees typically have large location and depth uncertainties. horizontalError Data Type Decimal Typical Val
comcat_column_documentation.dmin: dmin Data Type Decimal Typical Values [0.4, 7.1] Description Horizontal distance from the epicenter to the nearest station (in degrees). 1 degree is approximately 111.2 kilometers.
